title: CEOs crave keys to unlock productivity
full_text:
Business leaders say Australia’s regulatory web is a constraint on productivity and have implored Jim Chalmers to honour a promise to hack away at duplicative and pointless rules.
Coles chief executive Leah Weckert has to personally provide sign-off around the collection of cans and bottles as part of the container deposit scheme, for example. The scheme is enforced state by state and in some cases requires the CEO’s imprimatur.
“This is not a good use of time,” she said.
Ms Weckert shared this example of red tape overreach at ASIC’s annual forum in Sydney on Tuesday, where the federal Treasurer sought validation for Labor’s deregulation agenda.
“We are at a real crossroads as a nation right now, where we have to find a way to unlock productivity,” Ms Weckert said.
The economy is staggering under high inflation and sluggish growth. Artificial intelligence is providing the tools for automation, but its arrival is creating joblessness, and a low-growth economy offers few opportunities for people re-entering the workforce.
Executives say bold action on regulation is key to reviving productivity, and Dr Chalmers may not have gone far enough.
In this year’s federal budget, the government announced it would double the level at which companies had to report financial statements to the Australian Securities & Investments Commission, to $100m in revenue and $50m in assets. Dr Chalmers said this would slash $210m in regulation spend annually.
ASIC chair Sarah Court said less regulation should be the aspiration, but change should not be made for “change’s sake”.
“We have to be a lot better at doing things a lot more simpler,” she said. Ms Court also floated the prospect of regulatory intervention to deal with a rising tide of AI-related harm, as scams and frauds flourished with the new technology.
Dr Chalmers said the government was making climate-related financial disclosures “more efficient” and “slashing repetitive data requests”, cutting compliance costs by $1bn a year.
He gave Ms Court credit for reducing “unnecessary regulation” and cutting the number of reviews ASIC conducted of companies and business.
But the market regulator has plenty to do. On Tuesday, ASIC announced it would return to a review of the private credit sector, probing how lenders had responded to ASIC jawboning on valuations, liquidity and their conduct.
UBS Australia co-head Nick Hughes said Australia had to deliver regulatory clarity to companies and avoid creating a “closed domestic digital ecosystem”.
Ms Weckert urged policymakers to be sensitive to AI companies that would extract “rents” while contributing little to the country.
She told the ASIC forum there were many low-hanging opportunities that governments should consider to boost productivity and slash the regulatory burden.
Too many states had different versions of laws that aimed to achieve the same outcome, and she sought a harmonisation of these rules.
Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock expressed her concern that businesses were booking expectations of higher inflation for longer, and the central bank had to challenge this.
If not, there was a risk inflation would be anchored too high for too long. Bendigo Bank CEO Richard Fennell, speaking separately to The Australian, said he was worried about high inflation. He said Dr Chalmers’ commitment to cut red tape was encouraging, but the government should look to cut public spending and free up capacity in the private sector. Fiscal policy had been working against monetary settings this year, leading to five interest rate rises.
On Tuesday, Bendigo Bank announced it had completed moving 90,000 customers of RACQ Bank to its own technology systems.
This deal gave Bendigo Bank exposure to the fast-growing Queensland market, which was desirable in an economic downturn with its many safe customers commanding significant financial buffers.
Victoria is an increasingly troubled state for Bendigo Bank, echoing a gloomy picture conveyed by other lenders.
Major banks have broadly reported growing levels of distress and loan arrears, albeit coming off a low base. Mr Fenell said unemployment shocks were a key cause of problem loans for banks, rather than borrowers overextending themselves.
He said for most customers who got into trouble, they could still sell their homes at a profit.
Andrew Auerbach, who leads National Australia Bank’s business lending division, said demand for business loans was intact, despite executives’ frustration with the economy.
Collapsed retailer David Jones, and NSW home builder Bathla, which failed in August owing at least $3.8bn, were not NAB clients, but the bank had conducted a review against its whole portfolio for assurance. “It’s not markedly softer,” Mr Auerbach said of demand from NAB’s construction clients. “The business needs of what people are borrowing for don’t look much different than a year ago.”
